newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-European press sharply divided over Euro row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-European press sharply divided over Euro row.

text.p: European newspapers split along political lines in their reaction to France's request for more time to consider the stability pact intended to underpin European monetary union.
From the political right came charges that the move by French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's new socialist government was meant to derail monetary union.
"The reality is that this is an attempt to mobilise monetary and financial policy to push back unemployment," German's Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung daily said in an editorial.

"The idea of a stability pact, which Germany and France had great trouble in developing, was to prevent exactly this kind of misuse of financial policy," it said, adding that France's leaders had returned to the "economic thinking of the 1960s".
Left-leaning papers, on the other hand, saw the French action as justified and not necessarily a threat to the 1999 launch date for EMU.
The French daily Liberation, which strongly supports Jospin, said: "Yes, France has asked for a delay to think. But it has accepted the main point so it's not exactly what one would call a break-up.

"After such a clear vote in France and with Europe dominated by social democrats, the narrow free-market spirit which presided over the conclusion of the Maastricht Treaty must necessarily give in a bit," Liberation said.

The conservative Le Figaro, generally hostile to Jospin's government, wrote in an editorial that "the noose now tightening around the new cabinet's neck is that it must either honour its election promises and open a crisis with Europe or apply Europe's rules in France and provoke a rise in the country of disappointments whose consequences are impossible to predict."
In Germany, some commentators said France's proposal to think more about the pact was more than just a delaying tactic and that next week's European Union summit in Amsterdam was heading for crisis.

"If Paris seeks to put new elements into the stability pact that means nothing less than a delay (in EMU) as well as calling into question whether the stability pact will ever come about," the Handelsblatt business daily said.
The Bonn-based General Anzeiger daily said "a real crisis" was in the offing at the summit.

"(French Prime Minister) Lionel Jospin has put the fight against unemployment at the heart of his campaign. If he wants to remain credible he must demand other EU partners follow suit," it commented. "Therein lies his dilemma."
The left-leaning Frankfurter Rundschau disagreed.

"This (the French request for a delay) must be allowed and comes as no surprise as it is what the Socialists called for in their election campaign. The punctual launch of the euro would not yet be called into question by a delay in this agreement at Amsterdam," it said.

Italian commentators viewed the situation as a clash of two cultures, with the daily La Repubblica talking about a battle between France's "humanistic" approach and Germany's "materialistic" approach.

Adriana Cerretelli, writing in financial daily Il Sole, said Jospin, fresh from an election victory and with European voters swinging to the left, could press for a significant agreement with a Bonn government limited in its room to manoeuvre.

Countering a German diplomat who shoe quoted lamenting; "Why aren't the French capable of taking what's happening in Germany seriously?" Cerretelli asked, "Why aren't the Germans capable of understanding what's happening in the majority of other European countries?"
An Irish Times editorial said it was still likely that the move to monetary union will go ahead on schedule on January 1, 1999.

"However, it is far from certain...It may be that a compromise can be reached by inserting a commitment towards employment in the pact but Germany will resist any substantial watering down of its terms."
Spanish financial daily Gaceta de los Negocios highlighted market fears that the French move opened the door to a relaxation of the processes of budget deficit reduction from 1998 onwards.
"If the French government is really committed to monetary union, it must take some lessons on how markets work to avoid the single currency becoming more of a headache than it has already become."
In the UK, The Times said in an editorial; "If the German leader (Kohl) could swallow his pride, he would call for a delay in the rush toward EMU and our own government should back him."

The Guardian commented: "Europe's blinkered dash for a single currency, instead of co-ordinating economic policy, is putting the cart before the horse. The EU's pre-occupation with fiscal convergence has prevented it from exploiting the advantages of an integrated market."
The anti-European British tabloid Sun trumpeted what is saw as the demise of the Euro. "We said the single currency would end in tears. Yesterday it did -- for the Germans."
